 314: \subsection{Affine transfer to a shifted-weight residue model}\label{sec:stab:transfer}
 315: 
 316: We shall also compare the canonical residue-count function
 317: $d_m^\sharp$ with the shifted-weight residue-count function
 318: $\widetilde d_m$ from
 319: Definition~\ref{def:fiber-notation-and-residue-counts}.
 320: 
 321: \begin{lemma}[Fibonacci cross-multiplication modulo $F_{m+2}$]\label{lem:cross-multiplication}
 322: Extend the Fibonacci sequence by $F_0:=0$. Then for every $m\ge 1$ and $1\le j\le m$,
 323: \[
 324: F_{m+1}F_j \equiv (-1)^{j-1}F_{m+2-j}\pmod{F_{m+2}}.
 325: \]
 326: \end{lemma}
 327: 
 328: \begin{proof}
 329: Use d'Ocagne's identity
 330: \[
 331: F_uF_{v+1}-F_{u+1}F_v = (-1)^vF_{u-v}
 332: \]
 333: with $(u,v)=(m+1,j-1)$. This gives
 334: \[
 335: F_{m+1}F_j-F_{m+2}F_{j-1}=(-1)^{j-1}F_{m+2-j}.
 336: \]
 337: Reducing modulo $F_{m+2}$ proves the claim.
 338: \end{proof}
 339: 
 340: \begin{theorem}[Affine transfer principle]\label{thm:affine-transfer}
 341: For every $m\ge1$, define
 342: \[
 343: \pi_m:\ZZ/F_{m+2}\ZZ\longrightarrow \ZZ/F_{m+2}\ZZ,
 344: \qquad
 345: \pi_m(r):=F_{m+1}(r+1)-1.
 346: \]
 347: Then $\pi_m$ is a permutation and, for every residue
 348: $r\in\ZZ/F_{m+2}\ZZ$,
 349: \[
 350: \widetilde d_m(r)=d_m^\sharp(\pi_m(r)).
 351: \]
 352: Equivalently, the canonical and shifted-weight fiber models differ only by
 353: the affine relabeling $\pi_m$ of the residue circle.
 354: \end{theorem}
 355: 
 356: \begin{proof}
 357: Because consecutive Fibonacci numbers are coprime,
 358: $\gcd(F_{m+1},F_{m+2})=1$, multiplication by $F_{m+1}$ is a unit modulo
 359: $F_{m+2}$.  Hence $\pi_m$ is a permutation.
 360: 
 361: For $\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_m)\in\{0,1\}^m$, set
 362: \[
 363: (T_m\omega)_k=
 364: \begin{cases}
 365: \omega_{m+1-k}, & m+1-k\text{ is odd},\\
 366: 1-\omega_{m+1-k}, & m+1-k\text{ is even}.
 367: \end{cases}
 368: \]
 369: This defines a bijection $T_m:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}^m$.  By
 370: Lemma~\ref{lem:cross-multiplication},
 371: \[
 372: F_{m+1}\widetilde{\Val}_m(\omega)
 373: \equiv
 374: \sum_{j=1}^m \omega_j(-1)^{j-1}F_{m+2-j}
 375: \pmod {F_{m+2}}.
 376: \]
 377: For even $j$ replace $-\omega_j$ by $(1-\omega_j)-1$.  After the change of
 378: index $k=m+1-j$, this becomes
 379: \[
 380: F_{m+1}\widetilde{\Val}_m(\omega)
 381: \equiv
 382: \Val_m(T_m\omega)-C_m
 383: \pmod {F_{m+2}},
 384: \]
 385: where
 386: \[
 387: C_m:=\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\ j\ \mathrm{even}}} F_{m+2-j}.
 388: \]
 389: The elementary Fibonacci sum identity
 390: \[
 391: \sum_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\ j\ \mathrm{even}}} F_{m+2-j}=F_{m+1}-1
 392: \]
 393: follows by writing the sum as
 394: $F_{m}+F_{m-2}+\cdots$ when $m$ is even and as
 395: $F_{m-1}+F_{m-3}+\cdots$ when $m$ is odd, and applying
 396: $F_2+F_4+\cdots+F_{2q}=F_{2q+1}-1$ and
 397: $F_3+F_5+\cdots+F_{2q+1}=F_{2q+2}-1$.  Therefore
 398: \[
 399: \Val_m(T_m\omega)
 400: \equiv
 401: F_{m+1}\widetilde{\Val}_m(\omega)+F_{m+1}-1
 402: \pmod {F_{m+2}}.
 403: \]
 404: If $\widetilde{\Val}_m(\omega)\equiv r$, then
 405: \[
 406: \Val_m(T_m\omega)\equiv F_{m+1}(r+1)-1=\pi_m(r)
 407: \pmod {F_{m+2}}.
 408: \]
 409: Conversely, since $T_m$ is bijective and $\pi_m$ is a permutation, every raw
 410: word counted by $d_m^\sharp(\pi_m(r))$ arises uniquely in this way from a raw
 411: word counted by $\widetilde d_m(r)$.  Hence the two counts are equal.
 412: \end{proof}
 413: 
 414: \begin{corollary}[Transfer of multiset-based statistics]\label{cor:affine-transfer-stats}
 415: For every $m\ge1$, the shifted-weight model and the canonical model have the
 416: same unordered multiset of fiber sizes.  Consequently they have the same
 417: maximal fiber size, maximal-fiber multiplicity, second moment
 418: $\sum_xd_m(x)^2$, and every other statistic that depends only on the unordered
 419: fiber multiset.
 420: \end{corollary}
 421: 
 422: \begin{proof}
 423: Theorem~\ref{thm:affine-transfer} identifies the shifted residue-count
 424: function $\widetilde d_m$ with the canonical residue-count function
 425: $d_m^\sharp$ after applying the permutation $\pi_m$ of
 426: $\ZZ/F_{m+2}\ZZ$.  Permuting residue labels does not change the unordered
 427: multiset of values, and all listed quantities are functions of that multiset
 428: alone.
 429: \end{proof}
 430: 
 431: \begin{remark}[Closed form of the affine offset]
 432: The affine offset used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:affine-transfer} is
 433: \[
 434: C_m=F_{m+1}-1.
 435: \]
 436: Indeed, for $m=2q$ one has
 437: \[
 438: C_{2q}=F_2+F_4+\cdots+F_{2q}=F_{2q+1}-1=F_{m+1}-1,
 439: \]
 440: and for $m=2q+1$ one has
 441: \[
 442: C_{2q+1}=F_3+F_5+\cdots+F_{2q+1}=F_{2q+2}-1=F_{m+1}-1.
 443: \]
 444: Thus the affine transfer may also be written as
 445: \[
 446: \pi_m(r)=F_{m+1}(r+1)-1 \pmod{F_{m+2}}.
 447: \]
 448: \end{remark}

   1: \section{Finite-window Fibonacci stabilization}\label{sec:stabilization}
   2: 
   3: We now define the local arithmetic map. Stabilization reduces the Fibonacci valuation modulo $F_{m+2}$ and then selects the unique admissible representative. Its fibers are the finite objects behind both the threshold theorem and the two-window branch locus.
   4: 
   5: \subsection{Admissible language and Fibonacci valuation}\label{sec:stab:golden}
   6: 
   7: Let $(F_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be the Fibonacci sequence with $F_1=F_2=1$ and $F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n$.
   8: 
   9: \begin{definition}[Golden-mean legal language]\label{def:Xm}
  10: For $m\ge 1$, let
  11: \[
  12: X_m := \Bigl\{x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\{0,1\}^m : x_i x_{i+1}=0\ \text{for all }1\le i<m\Bigr\}.
  13: \]
  14: \end{definition}
  15: 
  16: \begin{definition}[Fibonacci valuation]\label{def:valuation}
  17: For $\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_m)\in\{0,1\}^m$, define
  18: \[
  19: \Val_m(\omega):=\sum_{k=1}^m \omega_k F_{k+1}.
  20: \]
  21: \end{definition}
  22: 
  23: \paragraph{Finite-window Zeckendorf range.}\label{prop:finite-window-range}
  24: For every $m\ge 1$, the restriction
  25: \[
  26: \Val_m|_{X_m}:X_m\longrightarrow \{0,1,\dots,F_{m+2}-1\}
  27: \]
  28: is a bijection.
  29: 
  30: \begin{proof}
  31: By Zeckendorf's theorem, every integer $N\ge 0$ has a unique expansion
  32: \[
  33: N=\sum_{k\ge 1}\varepsilon_k F_{k+1},\qquad \varepsilon_k\in\{0,1\},\qquad \varepsilon_k\varepsilon_{k+1}=0
  34: \]
  35: \cite{Zeckendorf1972,Lothaire2002}. If $0\le N < F_{m+2}$, then the largest Fibonacci weight that can appear is at most $F_{m+1}$, so the Zeckendorf expansion of $N$ has length at most $m$ and defines a unique element of $X_m$. Thus $\Val_m|_{X_m}$ is surjective.
  36: 
  37: To prove injectivity, let $x,y\in X_m$ with $\Val_m(x)=\Val_m(y)$. Then $x$ and $y$ are two Zeckendorf expansions of the same integer using weights up to $F_{m+1}$, hence $x=y$ by uniqueness.
  38: 
  39: Thus admissible words of length $m$ realize the residue classes $0,1,\dots,F_{m+2}-1$ exactly once.
  40: \end{proof}
  41: 
  42: \begin{remark}
  43: This finite-window range calculation is the form of Zeckendorf uniqueness
  44: that makes the stabilization map canonical at the right boundary. It is the
  45: finite-window counterpart of the finite-automaton normalization viewpoint
  46: for Fibonacci numeration developed in \cite{Frougny1992,Berstel2001}.
  47: \end{remark}
  48: 
  49: \subsection{Canonical finite-window stabilization}\label{sec:stab:fold}
  50: 
  51: \begin{definition}[Canonical stabilization map]\label{def:fold}
  52: For $m\ge1$, define
  53: \[
  54: \Fold_m:\{0,1\}^m\longrightarrow X_m
  55: \]
  56: by
  57: \[
  58: \Fold_m(\omega)
  59: :=
  60: \bigl(\Val_m|_{X_m}\bigr)^{-1}
  61: \Bigl(\Val_m(\omega)\pmod {F_{m+2}}\Bigr),
  62: \]
  63: where the residue is represented in $\{0,1,\ldots,F_{m+2}-1\}$.
  64: \end{definition}
  65: 
  66: \begin{remark}
  67: The map $\Fold_m$ is the finite-window canonicalization compatible with Fibonacci numeration: compute the raw Fibonacci-weighted value $\Val_m(\omega)$, reduce it modulo $F_{m+2}$, and write the residue in its unique length-$m$ Zeckendorf form. Local carry rewrites such as $11\mapsto 100$ realize the same residue-class operation.
  68: \end{remark}
  69: 
  70: \paragraph{Basic properties of $\Fold_m$.}\label{thm:fold-suite}
  71: For every $m\ge1$, the stabilization map of Definition~\ref{def:fold}
  72: satisfies the following canonicality properties.
  73: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  74:   \item $\Fold_m$ is well defined as a map
  75:   $\{0,1\}^m\to X_m$.
  76:   \item $\Fold_m$ is idempotent on admissible words:
  77:   $\Fold_m(x)=x$ for every $x\in X_m$.
  78:   \item $\Fold_m$ is surjective onto $X_m$.
  79:   \item The fibers
  80:   \[
  81:   \bigl\{\Fold_m^{-1}(\{x\}):x\in X_m\bigr\}
  82:   \]
  83:   form a disjoint partition of $\{0,1\}^m$.
  84: \end{enumerate}
  85: 
  86: \begin{proof}
  87: By the finite-window range calculation above, the restriction
  88: \[
  89: \Val_m|_{X_m}:X_m\longrightarrow \{0,\ldots,F_{m+2}-1\}
  90: \]
  91: is a bijection.  Hence every residue class represented in
  92: $\{0,\ldots,F_{m+2}-1\}$ has a unique admissible representative in $X_m$.
  93: For any raw word $\omega\in\{0,1\}^m$, the residue
  94: $\Val_m(\omega)\bmod F_{m+2}$ therefore has a unique preimage under
  95: $\Val_m|_{X_m}$, which is precisely the word denoted by $\Fold_m(\omega)$.
  96: This proves well-definedness.
  97: 
  98: If $x\in X_m$, then $\Val_m(x)$ already lies in
  99: $\{0,\ldots,F_{m+2}-1\}$ by that calculation.
 100: The unique admissible word with this residue is $x$ itself, so
 101: $\Fold_m(x)=x$.  This proves idempotence on $X_m$.  Surjectivity follows at
 102: once: for each $x\in X_m$, the preceding identity gives $x=\Fold_m(x)$.
 103: 
 104: Finally, every function partitions its domain into inverse images of points in
 105: its image.  Since the image of $\Fold_m$ is exactly $X_m$ by surjectivity, the
 106: nonempty fibers indexed by $x\in X_m$ are pairwise disjoint and their union is
 107: the whole cube $\{0,1\}^m$.
 108: \end{proof}

 113: \begin{definition}[Fiber and residue-count notation]\label{def:fiber-notation-and-residue-counts}
 114: For $m\ge1$ and $x\in X_m$, write
 115: \[
 116: \mathcal F_m(x):=\Fold_m^{-1}(\{x\})\subset\{0,1\}^m,
 117: \qquad
 118: d_m(x):=|\mathcal F_m(x)|.
 119: \]
 120: The calligraphic symbol distinguishes fibers from the Fibonacci number $F_m$.
 121: 
 122: For a residue $r\in\ZZ/F_{m+2}\ZZ$, represented by
 123: $0\le r<F_{m+2}$, let
 124: \[
 125: x_r:=\bigl(\Val_m|_{X_m}\bigr)^{-1}(r)\in X_m
 126: \]
 127: and set
 128: \[
 129: d_m^\sharp(r):=d_m(x_r).
 130: \]
 131: Finally define the shifted-weight valuation
 132: \[
 133: \widetilde{\Val}_m(\omega):=\sum_{j=1}^m \omega_j F_j
 134: \qquad\text{in }\ZZ/F_{m+2}\ZZ,
 135: \]
 136: and the corresponding shifted residue count
 137: \[
 138: \widetilde d_m(r):=
 139: \#\bigl\{\omega\in\{0,1\}^m:
 140: \widetilde{\Val}_m(\omega)\equiv r\pmod {F_{m+2}}\bigr\}.
 141: \]
 142: \end{definition}
 143: 
 144: \subsection{Residue fibers and Fourier formula}\label{sec:stab:fiber}
 145: 
 146: \begin{theorem}[Residue characterization of fibers and counts]\label{thm:fiber-residue}
 147: Let $x\in X_m$ and write
 148: \[
 149: r_x:=\Val_m(x)\in\{0,\ldots,F_{m+2}-1\}.
 150: \]
 151: Then
 152: \[
 153: \mathcal F_m(x)=
 154: \Bigl\{\omega\in\{0,1\}^m:
 155: \Val_m(\omega)\equiv r_x \pmod {F_{m+2}}\Bigr\}.
 156: \]
 157: Equivalently,
 158: \[
 159: d_m(x)=
 160: \#\Bigl\{\omega\in\{0,1\}^m:
 161: \sum_{k=1}^m\omega_kF_{k+1}\equiv r_x\pmod {F_{m+2}}\Bigr\}.
 162: \]
 163: Consequently, for every residue $r\in\ZZ/F_{m+2}\ZZ$,
 164: \[
 165: d_m^\sharp(r)=
 166: \#\Bigl\{\omega\in\{0,1\}^m:
 167: \Val_m(\omega)\equiv r\pmod {F_{m+2}}\Bigr\},
 168: \]
 169: and the residue-indexed families partition the full cube:
 170: \[
 171: \sum_{r\in\ZZ/F_{m+2}\ZZ} d_m^\sharp(r)
 172: =
 173: \sum_{r\in\ZZ/F_{m+2}\ZZ} \widetilde d_m(r)
 174: =2^m.
 175: \]
 176: \end{theorem}
 177: 
 178: \begin{proof}
 179: By Definition~\ref{def:fold},
 180: \[
 181: \Fold_m(\omega)=x
 182: \]
 183: holds exactly when
 184: \[
 185: \bigl(\Val_m|_{X_m}\bigr)^{-1}
 186: \Bigl(\Val_m(\omega)\pmod {F_{m+2}}\Bigr)=x.
 187: \]
 188: Since $\Val_m|_{X_m}$ is bijective by
 189: the finite-window range calculation, this is equivalent to
 190: \[
 191: \Val_m(\omega)\equiv\Val_m(x)\pmod {F_{m+2}}.
 192: \]
 193: Counting the raw words satisfying this congruence gives the formula for
 194: $d_m(x)$.
 195: 
 196: Now fix a residue $r$ and take $x=x_r$ from
 197: Definition~\ref{def:fiber-notation-and-residue-counts}.  Since
 198: $\Val_m(x_r)=r$, the preceding formula gives the displayed expression for
 199: $d_m^\sharp(r)$.  The congruence classes modulo $F_{m+2}$ form a disjoint
 200: partition of the possible values of $\Val_m(\omega)$ as
 201: $\omega$ ranges over $\{0,1\}^m$, so the sum of the canonical residue counts is
 202: $2^m$.  The same partition argument applied to the shifted valuation
 203: $\widetilde{\Val}_m$ gives
 204: $\sum_r\widetilde d_m(r)=2^m$.
 205: \end{proof}

 208: At $m=5$ the admissible language $X_5$ has $F_7=13$ words. The raw word $\omega=11010$ has valuation
 209: \[
 210: \Val_5(11010)=F_2+F_3+F_5=1+2+5=8.
 211: \]
 212: The unique admissible word of length five with residue $8$ modulo $13$ is $00001$, since $\Val_5(00001)=F_6=8$. Thus
 213: \[
 214: \Fold_5(11010)=00001.
 215: \]
 216: In fact
 217: \[
 218: \mathcal F_5(00001)=\{00001,\ 00110,\ 11010\}.
 219: \]
 220: This is the local ambiguity studied below. Isolated windows can fold together, but overlap removes the ambiguity for $m\ge3$.
 221: \end{remark}

   4: For $m\ge2$, define the one-sided sliding recoding by
   5: \[
   6: (\Phi_m^+(a))_t:=\Fold_m(a_t,\ldots,a_{t+m-1}),\qquad t\ge0,
   7: \]
   8: and its one-sided image by
   9: \[
  10: Y_m^+:=\Phi_m^+(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}).

  13: \begin{theorem}[Complete classification of the two-window branch locus]\label{thm:m2-branch-locus}
  14: Let
  15: \[
  16: y^\ast:=(\ldots,00,00,00,\ldots)\in Y_2.
  17: \]
  18: Then
  19: \[
  20: \Phi_2^{-1}(y^\ast)=\{0^{\ZZ},1^{\ZZ}\}.
  21: \]
  22: Every other point of $Y_2$ has a singleton preimage under $\Phi_2$.
  23: \end{theorem}
  24: 
  25: \begin{proof}
  26: For $m=2$ the modulus is $F_4=3$ and the two weights in $\Val_2$ are
  27: $F_2=1$ and $F_3=2$.  The legal words are
  28: \[
  29: X_2=\{00,10,01\},
  30: \]
  31: with residues
  32: \[
  33: \Val_2(00)=0,\qquad \Val_2(10)=1,\qquad \Val_2(01)=2.
  34: \]
  35: Thus these three legal words represent the three residue classes modulo $3$.
  36: For the four raw two-windows one obtains
  37: \[
  38: \Val_2(00)=0,\qquad
  39: \Val_2(10)=1,\qquad
  40: \Val_2(01)=2,\qquad
  41: \Val_2(11)=3\equiv0\pmod3.
  42: \]
  43: Applying Definition~\ref{def:fold} to these residues gives the complete
  44: two-window table
  45: \[
  46: \Fold_2(00)=00,\qquad \Fold_2(11)=00,\qquad
  47: \Fold_2(10)=10,\qquad \Fold_2(01)=01.
  48: \]
  49: Thus a symbol $10$ in the output determines the adjacent raw pair as $10$, a
  50: symbol $01$ determines the adjacent raw pair as $01$, and a symbol $00$ says
  51: precisely that the two adjacent raw bits are equal.
  52: 
  53: If $y=y^\ast$, then every adjacent raw pair in any lift must be either $00$ or
  54: $11$, so all adjacent raw bits are equal.  The only two lifts are therefore
  55: $0^{\ZZ}$ and $1^{\ZZ}$.
  56: 
  57: Now suppose $y\ne y^\ast$.  Choose an index $s$ with
  58: $y_s\in\{10,01\}$.  This output symbol determines the raw pair
  59: $(a_s,a_{s+1})$.  Moving to the right, each subsequent output symbol determines
  60: $a_{t+1}$ from $a_t$: if $y_t=00$ then $a_{t+1}=a_t$, while if
  61: $y_t=10$ or $01$ the pair is explicitly that symbol.  Moving to the left,
  62: the same rule determines $a_t$ from $a_{t+1}$.  Hence there is at most one
  63: bi-infinite lift.  Since $y\in Y_2$, at least one lift exists, so the lift is
  64: unique.
  65: \end{proof}

  68: % a separate supplement but are not used in the main proof chain.

  70: \begin{corollary}[Exact entropy and KL defect formulas at the two-window threshold]\label{cor:m2-defect-formulas}
  71: Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{\ZZ}$ and let
  72: $\eta:=(\Phi_2)_*\mu$.  Set
  73: \[
  74: B_0:=\{0^{\ZZ}\},\qquad B_1:=\{1^{\ZZ}\},\qquad
  75: p_i:=\mu(B_i),\qquad p:=p_0+p_1.
  76: \]
  77: Let $\mu=\int\mu_y\,d\eta(y)$ be a Rokhlin disintegration over $\Phi_2$,
  78: so that $\mu_y$ is supported on $\Phi_2^{-1}(y)$ for $\eta$-almost every
  79: $y$.  We use the convention
  80: \[
  81: H_\mu(\mathrm{Id}\mid\Phi_2)
  82: :=\int_{Y_2}H(\mu_y)\,d\eta(y),
  83: \]
  84: with extended value $+\infty$ allowed, although the formula below is finite.
  85: Then the conditional entropy of the raw trajectory given its stabilized
  86: trajectory is
  87: \[
  88: H_\mu(\mathrm{Id}\mid \Phi_2)=
  89: \begin{cases}
  90: 0, & p=0,\\[1mm]
  91: p\,h_2(p_0/p), & p>0,
  92: \end{cases}
  93: \]
  94: where $h_2(s):=-s\log s-(1-s)\log(1-s)$.
  95: 
  96: If $\nu$ is another Borel probability measure, $\xi:=(\Phi_2)_*\nu$,
  97: $q_i:=\nu(B_i)$ and $q:=q_0+q_1$, then, whenever the right-hand side is finite,
  98: \[
  99: D_{\KL}(\mu\|\nu)-D_{\KL}(\eta\|\xi)
 100: =
 101: p\,D_{\KL}\!\left(
 102: \left(\frac{p_0}{p},\frac{p_1}{p}\right)
 103: \middle\|
 104: \left(\frac{q_0}{q},\frac{q_1}{q}\right)
 105: \right),
 106: \]
 107: with the convention that the defect is $0$ when $p=0$.  If $p>0$ and $q=0$,
 108: then both $D_{\KL}(\mu\|\nu)$ and $D_{\KL}(\eta\|\xi)$ are infinite and no
 109: finite defect identity is asserted.  If $p>0$, $q>0$, and some $p_i>0=q_i$,
 110: then the raw divergence and the displayed defect are infinite.
 111: 
 112: Equivalently, in extended-value form: if $\eta\not\ll\xi$, then
 113: $D_{\KL}(\eta\|\xi)=+\infty$ and data processing forces
 114: $D_{\KL}(\mu\|\nu)=+\infty$, so no finite difference is formed. If
 115: $\eta\ll\xi$ but $\mu\not\ll\nu$, then $D_{\KL}(\mu\|\nu)=+\infty$ and the
 116: conditional defect is $+\infty$. If $\mu\ll\nu$ and hence $\eta\ll\xi$, the
 117: chain rule gives the finite or infinite nonnegative defect displayed above.
 118: \end{corollary}
 119: 
 120: \begin{proof}
 121: By Theorem~\ref{thm:m2-branch-locus}, the conditional distribution of $a$
 122: given $\Phi_2(a)=y$ is a point mass for every $y\ne y^\ast$.  Over
 123: $y^\ast$ it is the two-point distribution
 124: \[
 125: \left(\frac{p_0}{p},\frac{p_1}{p}\right)
 126: \]
 127: when $p>0$.  Integrating the entropy of these conditional distributions gives
 128: the displayed conditional-entropy formula.
 129: 
 130: Choose also a Rokhlin disintegration
 131: $\nu=\int\nu_y\,d\xi(y)$ over $\Phi_2$.  The relative-entropy chain rule for
 132: standard Borel spaces says that, if $\mu\ll\nu$ and hence $\eta\ll\xi$, then
 133: \[
 134: D_{\KL}(\mu\|\nu)
 135: =D_{\KL}(\eta\|\xi)
 136: +\int D_{\KL}\bigl(\mu(\,\cdot\,\mid \Phi_2=y)\|
 137: \nu(\,\cdot\,\mid \Phi_2=y)\bigr)\,d\eta(y),
 138: \]
 139: with values in $[0,+\infty]$.  If $\eta\not\ll\xi$, then
 140: $D_{\KL}(\eta\|\xi)=+\infty$ and necessarily $D_{\KL}(\mu\|\nu)=+\infty$ by
 141: data processing.  If $\eta\ll\xi$ but $\mu\not\ll\nu$, then the raw divergence
 142: is $+\infty$; the finite-defect identity is asserted only in the
 143: absolute-continuous cases stated above.  In the present map, all conditional
 144: divergences vanish off $y^\ast$ because both conditional measures are the same
 145: point mass there.  The only possible contribution is over $y^\ast$, where the
 146: conditional laws are the two displayed branch distributions.  This proves the
 147: formula and the stated boundary cases.
 148: \end{proof}

 150: \begin{corollary}[Asymptotic sufficiency off the branch fiber]\label{cor:m2-asymptotic-sufficiency}
 151: Let
 152: \[
 153: B:=B_0\cup B_1=\{0^{\ZZ},1^{\ZZ}\}.
 154: \]
 155: On $\{0,1\}^{\ZZ}\setminus B$ the map $\Phi_2$ is a Borel isomorphism onto
 156: $Y_2\setminus\{y^\ast\}$.  Consequently, for any family of probability laws
 157: $\{\mu_u:u\in\mathcal U\}$ satisfying $\mu_u(B)=0$ for all $u$, the raw
 158: path-space experiment and the stabilized path-space experiment
 159: $\{(\Phi_2)_*\mu_u:u\in\mathcal U\}$ are deterministically equivalent.  In
 160: particular all decision problems based on the full trajectory and the
 161: path-space KL divergence are preserved.  For each fixed $u$ and each fixed
 162: raw cylinder, the cylinder is recovered from a sufficiently large stabilized
 163: block with $\mu_u$-probability tending to one.
 164: \end{corollary}
 165: 
 166: \begin{proof}
 167: Theorem~\ref{thm:m2-branch-locus} gives a singleton fiber over every point of
 168: $Y_2\setminus\{y^\ast\}$ and shows that the whole non-singleton fiber is $B$.
 169: The graph rule in its proof reconstructs the unique raw sequence from any
 170: nonconstant output by locating one symbol $10$ or $01$ and propagating left and
 171: right; this gives a Borel inverse on $Y_2\setminus\{y^\ast\}$.  Thus $\Phi_2$
 172: is a measurable bijection between the two full-measure spaces for every
 173: $\mu_u$ in the family.  Transporting full-trajectory decision rules through
 174: this inverse gives identical risk distributions, and invariance of KL
 175: divergence under a bimeasurable change of variables gives the path-space KL
 176: claim.
 177: 
 178: It remains only to justify the stated asymptotic finite-window recovery.  To
 179: recover a fixed raw coordinate from a finite stabilized block, search inside
 180: that block for a symbol $10$ or $01$ and propagate the equality rule through

 succeeded in 182ms:
 181: the intervening $00$ symbols.  The only obstruction inside a symmetric
 182: stabilized block of radius $N$ is that all visible symbols in that block are
 183: $00$.  The corresponding raw event is the union of the two constant cylinders
 184: on an interval whose length tends to infinity with $N$; these events decrease
 185: to $B_0\cup B_1$.  Since $\mu_u(B)=0$, their probabilities tend to zero.  A
 186: finite raw cylinder is recovered by applying the same argument to finitely
 187: many coordinates and taking a union bound.
 188: \end{proof}

 190: \begin{corollary}[Mod-zero invertibility at the two-window threshold]\label{cor:m2-mod-zero}
 191: Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{\ZZ}$.  The map
 192: \[
 193: \Phi_2:(\{0,1\}^{\ZZ},\mu)\longrightarrow(Y_2,(\Phi_2)_*\mu)
 194: \]
 195: admits a measurable inverse modulo null sets if and only if
 196: \[
 197: \mu(\{0^{\ZZ}\})=0\quad\text{or}\quad \mu(\{1^{\ZZ}\})=0.
 198: \]
 199: In particular, if $\mu(\{0^{\ZZ},1^{\ZZ}\})=0$, then $\Phi_2$ is a mod-zero
 200: isomorphism.
 201: \end{corollary}
 202: 
 203: \begin{proof}
 204: If both branch atoms have positive $\mu$-mass, then every full-measure subset
 205: of the domain contains both $0^{\ZZ}$ and $1^{\ZZ}$, and these two points have
 206: the same image.  No inverse can be defined modulo null sets.
 207: 
 208: Conversely, suppose one of the two branch atoms is null.  Remove that null
 209: atom from the domain.  On the remaining full-measure set every fiber is a
 210: singleton by Theorem~\ref{thm:m2-branch-locus}: off $y^\ast$ this is the
 211: branch-locus classification, and over $y^\ast$ only the non-null branch atom
 212: remains.  The inverse is the Borel inverse from
 213: Corollary~\ref{cor:m2-asymptotic-sufficiency} off $y^\ast$, together with the
 214: remaining branch point at $y^\ast$ when it has positive mass.
 215: \end{proof}

 218: \paragraph{Full block complexity of the one-sided stabilized image.}\label{cor:one-sided-complexity}
 219: Let
 220: \[
 221: p_{Y_m^+}(n):=\#\mathcal L_n(Y_m^+)
 222: \]
 223: be the length-$n$ word complexity of the one-sided stabilized image
 224: $Y_m^+$.  If $m\ge3$ and $n\ge m$, then
 225: \[
 226: p_{Y_m^+}(n)=2^{n+m-1}.
 227: \]
 228: 
 229: \begin{proof}
 230: The length-$n$ words in $Y_m^+$ are exactly the image of the finite-block map
 231: \[
 232: \Phi_{m,n}:\{0,1\}^{n+m-1}\to X_m^n.
 233: \]
 234: The domain has cardinality $2^{n+m-1}$.  Since $m\ge3$ and $n\ge m$,
 235: Theorem~\ref{thm:block-invertibility} says that $\Phi_{m,n}$ is injective.
 236: Therefore its image, namely $\mathcal L_n(Y_m^+)$, has the same cardinality.
 237: \end{proof}
 238: 
 239: \paragraph{One-sided stabilized-window conjugacy.}\label{cor:one-sided-conjugacy}
 240: For every $m\ge3$, the map
 241: \[
 242: \Phi_m^+:\{0,1\}^{\NN}\longrightarrow Y_m^+
 243: \]
 244: is a topological conjugacy of one-sided shifts onto its image.  Its inverse is
 245: the sliding-block code
 246: \[
 247: (\Phi_m^+)^{-1}(y)_t=\psi_m(y_t,\ldots,y_{t+m-1}),
 248: \qquad t\ge0,
 249: \]
 250: with memory $0$ and anticipation $m-1$.
 251: 
 252: \begin{proof}
 253: Surjectivity onto $Y_m^+$ is the definition of the image.  The local formula
 254: in Section~\ref{sec:stab:conjugacy} applies to every one-sided trajectory
 255: because the block $(y_t,\ldots,y_{t+m-1})$ is available for each $t\ge0$.
 256: Thus it recovers every raw coordinate $a_t$.  The decoder is continuous and
 257: commutes with the one-sided shift, so it is a topological inverse to
 258: $\Phi_m^+$ on $Y_m^+$.
 259: \end{proof}
 260: 
 261: \paragraph{Two-sided finite-memory conjugacy and finite-type closure.}\label{thm:two-sided-conjugacy}
 262: Assume $m\ge3$.  Then:
 263: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
 264:   \item The factor map
 265:   \[
 266:   \Phi_m:(\{0,1\}^{\ZZ},\sigma)\longrightarrow(Y_m,\sigma)
 267:   \]
 268:   is a topological conjugacy.  Its inverse is
 269:   \[
 270:   \Phi_m^{-1}(y)_t=\psi_m(y_t,\ldots,y_{t+m-1}).
 271:   \]
 272:   \item Let $\mathcal B_m:=\mathcal L_m(Y_m)$ and, for
 273:   $W\in\mathcal B_m$, let $\Psi_{m,m}(W)\in\{0,1\}^{2m-1}$ be the unique
 274:   raw block with $\Phi_{m,m}(\Psi_{m,m}(W))=W$.  A sequence
 275:   $y\in(X_m)^{\ZZ}$ belongs to $Y_m$ if and only if every length-$m$ block
 276:   $W_t:=(y_t,\ldots,y_{t+m-1})$ lies in $\mathcal B_m$ and the decoded raw
 277:   blocks satisfy the overlap condition
 278:   \[
 279:   \Psi_{m,m}(W_t)_{1,\ldots,2m-2}
 280:   =
 281:   \Psi_{m,m}(W_{t+1})_{0,\ldots,2m-3}
 282:   \qquad\text{for all }t\in\ZZ.
 283:   \]
 284:   \item In particular $Y_m$ is a subshift of finite type.  It is defined by
 285:   finitely many forbidden words of length at most $m+1$ over the alphabet
 286:   $X_m$.
 287:   \item Pushforward by $\Phi_m$ gives a bijection between shift-invariant
 288:   Borel probability measures on $\{0,1\}^{\ZZ}$ and shift-invariant Borel
 289:   probability measures on $Y_m$, with inverse pushforward by the displayed
 290:   local decoder.
 291: \end{enumerate}
 292: 
 293: \begin{proof}
 294: The explicit decoder in Section~\ref{sec:stab:conjugacy} gives a continuous
 295: shift-commuting left inverse to $\Phi_m$ on $Y_m$.  Since $Y_m$ is the image of
 296: $\Phi_m$, this left inverse is also a right inverse on $Y_m$.  Hence $\Phi_m$
 297: is a topological conjugacy, proving (i).
 298: 
 299: If $y=\Phi_m(a)$, then each $W_t$ lies in $\mathcal B_m$ and
 300: $\Psi_{m,m}(W_t)=a_ta_{t+1}\ldots a_{t+2m-2}$.  Consecutive decoded raw
 301: blocks therefore overlap in their common $2m-2$ coordinates, so the condition
 302: in (ii) is necessary.
 303: 
 304: Conversely, suppose a sequence $y\in(X_m)^{\ZZ}$ satisfies the two conditions
 305: in (ii).  The overlap condition glues the finite words
 306: $\Psi_{m,m}(W_t)$ into a unique bi-infinite binary sequence $a$ such that
 307: \[
 308: \Psi_{m,m}(W_t)=a_ta_{t+1}\ldots a_{t+2m-2}
 309: \qquad\text{for all }t.
 310: \]
 311: Applying $\Phi_{m,m}$ to this raw block gives $W_t$, so in particular
 312: \[
 313: \Fold_m(a_t,\ldots,a_{t+m-1})=y_t
 314: \]
 315: for every $t$.  Thus $y=\Phi_m(a)\in Y_m$.  This proves (ii).
 316: 
 317: The criterion in (ii) depends only on adjacent length-$m$ output blocks, hence
 318: only on words of length $m+1$ over the finite alphabet $X_m$.  There are
 319: finitely many violations, so $Y_m$ is an SFT with memory at most $m$.  This
 320: proves (iii).
 321: 
 322: Finally, a topological conjugacy sends invariant Borel probability measures
 323: bijectively to invariant Borel probability measures by pushforward, and the
 324: inverse bijection is pushforward by the inverse conjugacy.  The inverse
 325: conjugacy is the local decoder in (i), proving (iv).
 326: \end{proof}
 327: 
 328: \begin{remark}[Decoder complexity]\label{rem:decoder-complexity}
 329: The inverse code supplied above reads a
 330: sliding window of length $m$ and outputs one raw bit. Equivalently, the decoder
 331: may be implemented by maintaining an overlap state of size $m-1$. The
 332: arithmetic cost is $O(m)$ per output symbol, since each decoding step involves
 333: at most $m$ Fibonacci-weighted additions modulo $F_{m+2}$.
 334: \end{remark}
 335: 
 336: \begin{remark}\label{rem:exact-recoding}
 337: For $m\ge3$ the stabilized image is a subshift of finite type topologically
 338: conjugate to the full two-shift by a finite-memory code. The only obstruction
 339: below threshold is the branch locus in Theorem~\ref{thm:m2-branch-locus}.
 340: \end{remark}
 341: 
 342: \begin{remark}\label{rem:sofic-comparison}
 343: In the terminology of \cite{LindMarcus1995}, $\mathcal G_m$ is a
 344: right-resolving presentation of the sofic shift $Y_m$, and $\Phi_m$ has degree
 345: at most $2^{m-1}$ by the finite-state lift above. A right-resolving
 346: factor of degree~1 between irreducible shifts of finite type is a conjugacy
 347: \cite[Theorem~8.1.16]{LindMarcus1995}; see also \cite{Ashley1991} for the
 348: equal-entropy resolving theory and \cite{Boyle1983} for the lower-entropy
 349: obstruction. The threshold theorem says that degree~1 is achieved exactly at
 350: $m=3$. This is an arithmetic fact, not a formal consequence of the sofic
 351: framework, and it uses the explicit decoder of Lemma~\ref{lem:m3-decoder}.
 352: \end{remark}

\section{Routine dynamical consequences}\label{sec:supp-routine-dynamics}

This section records standard consequences removed from the main article.
They are not inputs to the arithmetic threshold or Fischer-cover arguments.

\begin{proposition}[Dynamical corollaries above threshold]
\label{prop:conjugacy-consequences}
For $m\ge3$, the conjugacy $\Phi_m$ identifies invariant Borel probability
measures on the full two-shift and on $Y_m$, preserving ergodicity, mixing
properties, Bernoulli-ness, the $K$-property, and entropy.  Moreover,
\[
\#\operatorname{Fix}(\sigma^n|_{Y_m})=2^n,
\qquad
\zeta_{Y_m}(z)=\frac1{1-2z}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Section~\ref{sec:stab:branch-and-conjugacy} supplies a topological conjugacy and a
sliding-block inverse.  The measure correspondence and the listed
measure-theoretic properties are standard conjugacy invariants.  Period-$n$
points correspond bijectively to the $2^n$ period-$n$ points of the full
two-shift, and substitution in the Artin--Mazur definition gives
\[
\exp\left(\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{2^nz^n}{n}\right)=(1-2z)^{-1}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Entropy preservation for every aperture]
\label{prop:measure-entropy-preservation}
Let $m\ge2$, let $\nu$ be shift invariant on $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$, and put
$\eta=(\Phi_m)_*\nu$.  Then $h_\eta(\sigma)=h_\nu(\sigma)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For a raw block $A_{0:n+m-2}$ and its output block $Y_{0:n-1}$,
determinism and the resolving lift in Section~\ref{sec:stab:conjugacy} give
\[
0\le H_\nu(A_{0:n+m-2})-H_\eta(Y_{0:n-1})
\le(m-1)\log2.
\]
Indeed, after the initial $(m-1)$-bit overlap state is specified, the output
block determines the raw block.  Division by $n$ and passage to the limit
prove the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Topological entropy]
\label{cor:entropy-preservation}
For every $m\ge2$, $h_{\rm top}(Y_m)=\log2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The factor inequality gives the upper bound.  Applying
Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-entropy-preservation} to the fair Bernoulli law
and then the variational principle gives the lower bound.
\end{proof}

\section{Cyclic rank recoding for quadratic Pisot languages}
\label{sec:quadratic-pisot-extension}

The point requiring care is that a quadratic Pisot number need not be a unit
and its conjugate need not be negative.  Consequently the boundary-modified
constant-type language is not the appropriate common object.  We instead use
the greedy $\beta$-language and its canonical Parry--Bertrand positional rank.
This rank belongs to the established theory of nonintegral-base numeration
\cite{BertrandMathis1989,BruyereHansel1997,LecomteRigo2001}; the
canonical/noncanonical distinction for simple-Parry systems is clarified in
\cite{CharlierCisterninoStipulanti2022}.  We give a direct interval proof for
the two quadratic chambers because the exact endpoints are used later.  The
operation introduced here begins only when the fixed-length rank is reduced
cyclically modulo $Q_m$ and consecutive windows are overlapped.  This
recoding is not numerical
$\beta$-value normalization: it asserts congruence only between integer
language ranks and does not assert equality in $\mathbb Z[\beta]$.  The
classical $\beta$-shift and automata literature supplies context
\cite{Renyi1957,ItoTakahashi1974,Parry1960,Blanchard1989,Loraud1995};
the map-specific sliding-congruence statements used below are proved here.

\subsection{Quadratic classification and canonical finite windows}

\begin{lemma}[The two quadratic Pisot parameter chambers]
\label{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers}
Let $\beta>1$ be a quadratic algebraic integer and let $\beta'$ be its
conjugate.  Then $|\beta'|<1$ if and only if the minimal polynomial of
$\beta$ belongs to exactly one of the following two families:
\begin{align*}
P^-_{a,b}(x)&=x^2-ax-b, & a\ge b\ge1,\\
P^+_{a,b}(x)&=x^2-ax+b, & a\ge3,\quad 1\le b\le a-2.
\end{align*}
In the first chamber $\beta'<0$, $\lfloor\beta\rfloor=a$, and
\[
d_\beta(1)=ab0^\infty,\qquad
d_\beta^*(1)=\bigl(a(b-1)\bigr)^\infty.
\]
In the second chamber $\beta'>0$, $\lfloor\beta\rfloor=a-1$, and
\[
d_\beta(1)=(a-1)(a-b-1)^\infty=d_\beta^*(1).
\]
Here $d_\beta$ is the greedy expansion and $d_\beta^*$ is Parry's
quasi-greedy boundary word.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write the monic minimal polynomial as $x^2-ax+c$.  Since
$c=\beta\beta'\ne0$, the sign of $c$ is the sign of $\beta'$.  If
$c=-b<0$, then $b/\beta=|\beta'|<1$.  The positive root exceeds $a$;
the last inequality is equivalent, for integral $a,b$, to $1\le b\le a$.
Conversely these inequalities place the negative root in $(-1,0)$.
If $c=b>0$, then $0<b/\beta=\beta'<1$ and $a-1<\beta<a$; evaluating
$P^+_{a,b}$ at $a-1$ and $a$ gives exactly $a\ge3$ and
$1\le b\le a-2$.  The converses follow from the same sign test.

For $P^-_{a,b}$ one has $\beta^2=a\beta+b$.  The greedy algorithm applied
to $1$ therefore gives the two digits $a,b$ and then terminates; Parry's
standard replacement of a finite expansion gives
$d_\beta^*(1)=(a(b-1))^\infty$.  For $P^+_{a,b}$, put
$r=\beta-a+1=1-b/\beta$.  Then
$\lfloor\beta\rfloor=a-1$ and
\[
\beta r=\beta-b=(a-b-1)+r,
\]
so every digit after the first is $a-b-1$.  The expansion is infinite and
hence already quasi-greedy.  This is precisely Parry's calculation
\cite{Parry1960}; it is included to fix the parameters, not as a proof of
his general admissibility theorem.
\end{proof}

For either chamber put $d=\lfloor\beta\rfloor$ and
$\mathcal A_\beta=\{0,\ldots,d\}$.  Let $\mathcal L_m(X_\beta)$ be the
length-$m$ language of the two-sided greedy $\beta$-shift, characterized by
Parry's suffix inequalities against $d_\beta^*(1)$.

For words $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$ and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)$ in low-to-high
orientation, write $x<_{\rm colex}y$ when
$(x_m,\ldots,x_1)<_{\rm lex}(y_m,\ldots,y_1)$.  Lexicographic comparison of a
finite word with an infinite boundary uses the available finite prefix: the
first unequal digit decides the comparison, and equality through the end of
the finite word is allowed.  A comparison with $c_0^m$ is the literal
finite-word comparison.

\begin{definition}[Cyclic rank recoding attached to the Parry language]
\label{def:quadratic-parry-fold}
For $m\ge0$ define $Q_m(\beta)=|\mathcal L_m(X_\beta)|$; the recurrences for
these counts are proved in Proposition~\ref{prop:parry-rank-bijection}.
Use the low-to-high orientation
\[
X_m^{(\beta)}:=\{x\in\mathcal A_\beta^m:
(x_m,\ldots,x_1)\in\mathcal L_m(X_\beta)\}
\]
and set
\[
\operatorname{Rank}_{\beta,m}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}x_{j+1}Q_j(\beta).
\]
The cyclic language-rank recoding is
\[
\Fold_{\beta,m}(w)=
\bigl(\operatorname{Rank}_{\beta,m}|_{X_m^{(\beta)}}\bigr)^{-1}
\left(\operatorname{Rank}_{\beta,m}(w)\bmod Q_m(\beta)\right).
\]
Finally,
\[
(\Phi_{\beta,m}(z))_t
=\Fold_{\beta,m}(z_t,\ldots,z_{t+m-1}),\qquad
Y_{\beta,m}=\Phi_{\beta,m}(\mathcal A_\beta^{\mathbb Z}).
\]
The nontrivial overlap threshold is
\[
m_*(\beta)=\min\{m\ge2:\Phi_{\beta,m}\text{ is a conjugacy onto the
SFT }Y_{\beta,m}\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Canonical Parry--Bertrand rank in two quadratic chambers]
\label{prop:parry-rank-bijection}
The language counts satisfy
\begin{align}
Q_0&=1,\quad Q_1=a+1,\quad Q_m=aQ_{m-1}+bQ_{m-2}
&& (P^-_{a,b},\ m\ge2),\label{eq:qminus}\\
Q_0&=1,\quad Q_1=a,\quad Q_m=aQ_{m-1}-bQ_{m-2}
&& (P^+_{a,b},\ m\ge2).\label{eq:qplus}
\end{align}
For every quadratic Pisot $\beta$ and $m\ge1$,
\[
\operatorname{Rank}_{\beta,m}|_{X_m^{(\beta)}}:
X_m^{(\beta)}\longrightarrow\{0,\ldots,Q_m(\beta)-1\}
\]
is an order-preserving bijection when $X_m^{(\beta)}$ is read in the
colexicographic order.  This is the canonical Parry--Bertrand positional
rank; the proof below is a direct two-chamber interval proof of that standard
structure.  Thus Definition~\ref{def:quadratic-parry-fold} is
determined by the greedy language and its Parry word; it is not a choice of
an auxiliary enumeration.  For $P^-_{a,1}$ it is exactly the constant-type
metallic rank data recorded in Section~\ref{sec:metallic-cover}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
In the negative chamber, Parry admissibility reduces in the low-to-high
orientation to
\[
x_k=a\Longrightarrow x_{k-1}<b.
\]
We use induction on $m$, with the invariant that the ranks of $X_m^{(\beta)}$
form the initial interval $[0,Q_m-1]$.  It is immediate for $m=0,1$.  For
$m\ge2$, a high digit $h\in\{0,\ldots,a-1\}$ leaves an arbitrary word of
$X_{m-1}^{(\beta)}$ and hence contributes
\[
[hQ_{m-1},(h+1)Q_{m-1}-1].
\]
For high digit $a$, the next digit is
$g\in\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$ and the remaining word is arbitrary in
$X_{m-2}^{(\beta)}$; its ranks are
\[
aQ_{m-1}+[gQ_{m-2},(g+1)Q_{m-2}-1].
\]
The intervals are consecutive in colexicographic order and their union is
$[0,aQ_{m-1}+bQ_{m-2}-1]$.  This proves simultaneously the negative
recurrence, the induction invariant, and order preservation.

For the positive chamber put
\[
d=a-1,\qquad c_0=a-b-1,
\]
and define the boundary-bounded sublanguage
\[
B_m:=\{x\in X_m^{(\beta)}:
(x_m,\ldots,x_1)\le_{\rm lex}c_0^m\},
\qquad R_m:=|B_m|.
\]
We prove simultaneously, for every $m\ge0$, the coupled induction invariant
\begin{equation}
\Rank_{\beta,m}(X_m^{(\beta)})=[0,Q_m-1],
\qquad
\Rank_{\beta,m}(B_m)=[0,R_m-1].
\label{eq:coupled-rank-invariant}
\end{equation}
Here $X_0^{(\beta)}=B_0=\{\varnothing\}$, so $Q_0=R_0=1$ and the assertion
holds at $m=0$.  At $m=1$, one has $Q_1=d+1=a$ and
$R_1=c_0+1=a-b$, and the ranks are the stated intervals.

Assume \eqref{eq:coupled-rank-invariant} through length $m-1$.  Parry
admissibility says that a high digit $h<d$ may be followed by any word in
$X_{m-1}^{(\beta)}$, whereas a high digit $d$ must be followed by a word in
$B_{m-1}$.  The classes $h=0,\ldots,d-1$ therefore give the consecutive
intervals
\[
[hQ_{m-1},(h+1)Q_{m-1}-1],
\]
and the high class $h=d$ gives
\[
[dQ_{m-1},dQ_{m-1}+R_{m-1}-1].
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}
Q_m=dQ_{m-1}+R_{m-1},
\qquad
\Rank_{\beta,m}(X_m^{(\beta)})=[0,Q_m-1].
\label{eq:positive-X-coupling}
\end{equation}

The same decomposition inside $B_m$ has high digits
$0,\ldots,c_0-1$ followed by arbitrary words of $X_{m-1}^{(\beta)}$, and
high digit $c_0$ followed by a word of $B_{m-1}$.  Hence
\begin{equation}
R_m=c_0Q_{m-1}+R_{m-1},
\qquad
\Rank_{\beta,m}(B_m)=[0,R_m-1].
\label{eq:positive-B-coupling}
\end{equation}
This closes the simultaneous induction and proves consecutiveness rather than
assuming it.  Subtracting \eqref{eq:positive-B-coupling} from
\eqref{eq:positive-X-coupling} gives
\[
Q_m-R_m=(d-c_0)Q_{m-1}=bQ_{m-1}.
\]
Thus, for $m\ge2$,
\[
R_{m-1}=Q_{m-1}-bQ_{m-2}
\]
and
\[
Q_m=dQ_{m-1}+R_{m-1}
=(d+1)Q_{m-1}-bQ_{m-2}
=aQ_{m-1}-bQ_{m-2},
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:qplus}.  The order of the displayed digit classes is
the colexicographic order, so the same induction proves order preservation.
When $b=1$ in the negative chamber, the rule and recurrence are precisely
the metallic specialization recorded in Section~\ref{sec:metallic-cover}.
\end{proof}

\input{sections/05b_quadratic_pisot_local_structure}


 succeeded in 187ms:
\subsection{Arithmetic identifiability and optimal local structure}

The threshold classification leaves three finer questions: whether a fixed
aperture identifies the parameter chamber, how many consecutive output
symbols are needed by a future-only inverse, and whether the finite-block and
finite-type bounds in Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold} are
sharp.  We answer the first and third completely.  For the future-only
inverse question we
obtain the exact positive-chamber value and the exact negative-chamber value
at aperture three; the parameter-uniform negative-chamber value at larger
apertures remains an explicit interface.

\begin{theorem}[Aperture-two chamber duality and first separation]
\label{thm:quadratic-aperture-two-duality}
Let $q\ge3$ and $2\le\kappa\le q-1$, and let
\begin{align*}
\beta^-_{q,\kappa}&>1,
& (\beta^-_{q,\kappa})^2-(q-1)\beta^-_{q,\kappa}-\kappa&=0,\\
\beta^+_{q,\kappa}&>1,
& (\beta^+_{q,\kappa})^2-q\beta^+_{q,\kappa}+(q-\kappa)&=0.
\end{align*}
After identifying both digit alphabets with $\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$, their
aperture-two legal languages, ranks, folds, and sliding recodings coincide
pointwise.  Explicitly,
\[
Q_0=1,\qquad Q_1=q,\qquad Q_2=q(q-1)+\kappa,
\]
and
\[
X_2=\{(u,v):v<q-1\ \hbox{or}\ u<\kappa\},
\qquad
\Fold_2(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
(u,v),&v<q-1\ \hbox{or}\ u<\kappa,\\
(u-\kappa,0),&v=q-1\ \hbox{and}\ u\ge\kappa.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover, these are all cross-chamber coincidences at aperture two: the pair
$(q,\kappa)$ is recovered from the digit alphabet and the fold, and its
equivalence class contains the displayed negative- and positive-conjugate
bases when $\kappa\ge2$.  For $\kappa=1$ only the negative-conjugate member
is a quadratic Pisot base in the parameter ranges of
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers}.

The ambiguity is first resolved at aperture three.  In low-to-high
orientation,
\[
X_3^{(\beta^-_{q,\kappa})}
 \setminus X_3^{(\beta^+_{q,\kappa})}
=\{(h,\kappa-1,q-1):\kappa\le h\le q-1\},
\]
the reverse difference is empty, and
\[
Q_3(\beta^-_{q,\kappa})-Q_3(\beta^+_{q,\kappa})=q-\kappa.
\]
Thus the complete aperture-two input--output map does not determine the sign
of the conjugate, whereas the aperture-three legal language does.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For the negative chamber take $(a,b)=(q-1,\kappa)$; for the positive chamber
take $(a,b)=(q,q-\kappa)$.  The stated parameter bounds are precisely those
which place both choices in Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers}.  In both
cases $d=q-1$, while Proposition~\ref{prop:parry-rank-bijection} gives
\[
Q_2=(q-1)q+\kappa=q^2-(q-\kappa).
\]
The two length-two Parry conditions both say that a high digit $q-1$ must be
followed, in the low-to-high convention, by a digit smaller than $\kappa$.
The displayed fold now follows directly from cyclic reduction of
$u+qv$ modulo $Q_2$.  This proves pointwise equality of the two sliding maps.

Conversely, the alphabet gives $q$, and the least $u$ for which
$(u,q-1)$ is sent to $(0,0)$ gives $\kappa$.  The chamber parametrization in
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-pisot-chambers} then leaves exactly the two displayed
members when $\kappa\ge2$ and only the negative member when $\kappa=1$.

Finally, the two quasi-greedy boundary words are
\[
d_{\beta^-}^*(1)=((q-1)(\kappa-1))^\infty,
\qquad
d_{\beta^+}^*(1)=(q-1)(\kappa-1)^\infty.
\]
Their first two digits agree.  At length three, the negative boundary permits
a suffix $(q-1,\kappa-1,h)$ for every $h\le q-1$, whereas the positive
boundary requires $h\le\kappa-1$.  All other suffix tests agree.  Reversing
to the low-to-high convention gives exactly the stated set difference.
There are $q-\kappa$ such words.  Equivalently, the two recurrences give
\[
Q_3^-=(q-1)Q_2+\kappa q,\qquad
Q_3^+=qQ_2-(q-\kappa)q,
\]
whose difference is $q^2-Q_2=q-\kappa$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Open negative-chamber two-window interface]
\label{rem:negative-two-window-open-interface}
For $a\ge b\ge1$ and $m\ge4$, the natural candidate statement is that two
consecutive congruences
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}Q_je_j\equiv
\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}Q_je_{j+1}\equiv0\pmod{Q_m},
\qquad |e_j|\le a,
\]
force $e_0=0$ for the recurrence
$Q_{j+2}=aQ_{j+1}+bQ_j$.  Finite enumeration supports this assertion, but a
parameter-uniform proof requires an exhaustive bounded-carry invariant.  In
particular, sorting only by the two multiples of $Q_m$ and then appealing to
the signs of successive quotient coefficients does not prove that all carry
branches have been covered.  We therefore do not use or claim this candidate
statement below.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Future-only inverse bounds and the positive-chamber optimum]
\label{thm:quadratic-optimal-causal-inverse}
For $m\ge3$ define
\[
\ell_{\rm cau}(\beta,m)
=\min\{\ell\ge1:\ a_t=\psi(y_t,\ldots,y_{t+\ell-1})
\text{ for every }y=\Phi_{\beta,m}(a)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\ell_{\rm cau}(\beta,m)=3\quad(\beta'>0),
\qquad
\ell_{\rm cau}(\beta,3)=2\quad(\beta'<0).
\]
For $\beta'<0$ and $m\ge4$, the proved bounds are
\[
2\le \ell_{\rm cau}(\beta,m)\le m.
\]

If, explicitly, $(P)\subset\mathbb Z[z]$ denotes the principal ideal
generated by $P$ and
\[
\mathfrak a(P,d)=\min\{\deg H:0\ne H\in(P),\ H(0)\ne0,
\ \max_j|[z^j]H|\le d\},
\]
then
\[
\mathfrak a(P^-_{a,b},a)=2,
\qquad
\mathfrak a(P^+_{a,b},a-1)=3.
\]
Thus $\ell_{\rm cau}=\mathfrak a$ in the positive chamber for every
$m\ge3$ and in the negative chamber at $m=3$; equality in the negative
chamber for $m\ge4$ is precisely the interface in
Remark~\ref{rem:negative-two-window-open-interface}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose first that $P=P^-_{a,b}$, so $d=a$.  The coefficient vector
$(b,a,-1)$ of $-P$ is the difference of two digit blocks and has nonzero
first coordinate.  Padding it by zeros gives two raw length-$m$ words with
the same single output, so one output never suffices.  Conversely, equality
of two consecutive outputs at $m=3$ gives two overlapping triples from the
complete negative-chamber list in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences}.  A triple in that list with
nonzero first coordinate is necessarily $\pm(b,a,-1)$; the next triple would
then begin with $\pm(a,-1)$, which is not the initial pair of any triple in
the list.  Hence $e_0=0$, and two outputs determine the first digit at
$m=3$.  For $m\ge4$, the lower bound remains two, while
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences} shows that $m$ consecutive
outputs determine the entire overlapping raw block and hence its first digit.

Now let $P=P^+_{a,b}$, so $d=a-1$.  The polynomial
\[
(1+z)P(z)=b+(b-a)z+(1-a)z^2+z^3
\]
has all coefficients in $[-d,d]$ and nonzero constant term.  Its positive
and negative parts, padded by zeros, give two raw blocks with different first
digits and the same two consecutive outputs.  Indeed, the first weighted sum
is zero when $m\ge4$ and is $-Q_3$ when $m=3$, while the shifted sum is zero.
Thus two outputs do not suffice.

Three outputs do suffice.  For $m=3$ this is
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences}.  For $m\ge4$, apply the
elimination leading to \eqref{eq:quadratic-elimination} to the first three
equal-output congruences.  Since here $s=-1$ and $\delta=0$, it gives
\[
e_0+bQ_{m-1}e_{m+1}\equiv0\pmod{Q_m}.
\]
If $e_{m+1}\ne0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:nearest-multiple-separation} makes the
distance of the second term from $Q_m\mathbb Z$ at least
$Q_{m-2}>a-1\ge|e_0|$, a contradiction.  Hence $e_{m+1}=0$, and then
$|e_0|<Q_m$ forces $e_0=0$.

Finally, no nonzero polynomial of degree below two belongs to $(P_\beta)$.
For $P^-_{a,b}$ the polynomial $-P^-_{a,b}$ has coefficient norm $a$, so
$\mathfrak a(P^-_{a,b},a)=2$.  For $P^+_{a,b}$ every degree-two member of
the integral ideal is a nonzero integral multiple of $P^+_{a,b}$ and has
coefficient norm at least $a>d$, while $(1+z)P^+_{a,b}$ has coefficient norm
at most $a-1$.  Hence $\mathfrak a(P^+_{a,b},a-1)=3$, proving the last
assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Critical two-fixed-point normal form]
\label{thm:quadratic-critical-normal-form}
Let $\beta$ be an extremizer in
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold}, put
$q=\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1$ and $d=q-1$, and consider its critical map
$\Phi_{\beta,2}$.  Then
\[
\Fold_{\beta,2}(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
(u,v),&(u,v)\ne(d,d),\\
(0,0),&(u,v)=(d,d).
\end{cases}
\]
Its only nonsingleton two-sided fiber is
\[
\Phi_{\beta,2}^{-1}((00)^{\mathbb Z})
=\{0^{\mathbb Z},d^{\mathbb Z}\}.
\]
Consequently
\[
h_{\rm top}(Y_{\beta,2})=\log q,
\qquad
\#\operatorname{Fix}(\sigma^n|_{Y_{\beta,2}})=q^n-1,
\qquad
\zeta_{Y_{\beta,2}}(z)=\frac{1-z}{1-qz}.
\]
The critical image is strictly sofic.  Its right Fischer cover has vertices
$0,\ldots,d$ and one edge $u\to v$ for every ordered pair; the edge label is
$(u,v)$ except that $d\to d$ is labeled $(0,0)$.  The cover is bi-resolving,
and the factor is one-to-one away from the two fixed points above.  Hence, in
the standard terminology, the critical image is a near-Markov AFT shift and
its multiplicity graph is $K_{2,1}$: the two exceptional domain orbits lie
over the single exceptional image orbit.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
At either extremal locus the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold} has $\kappa=d$, which gives
the displayed rule.  Every nonzero output symbol records its raw edge
uniquely and hence propagates the raw digits uniquely in both directions.
If every output symbol is $(0,0)$, each raw edge is either $0\to0$ or
$d\to d$; overlap forces one of the two constant paths.  This proves the
fiber statement.

The map is finite-to-one from the full $q$-shift, so entropy is $\log q$.
A point fixed by $\sigma^n$ outside the exceptional image has a unique
preimage and that preimage is fixed by $\sigma^n$.  The $q^n$ fixed points
of the full shift therefore map to $q^n-1$ fixed image points, since exactly
the two constant preimages are identified.  The zeta identity follows from
\[
\exp\left(\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(q^n-1)z^n}{n}\right)
=\frac{1-z}{1-qz}.
\]

The displayed graph is right- and left-resolving and follower-separated.
Every vertex is reached by a one-symbol label different from $(0,0)$, which
is intrinsically synchronizing.  The standard Fischer-cover characterization
for an essential irreducible, right-resolving, follower-separated
presentation whose states are reached by intrinsically synchronizing words
therefore identifies it as the right Fischer cover
\cite{Fischer1975,Krieger1984,LindMarcus1995}.

To see that the image is not an SFT, fix $N$ and choose $L>N$.  The word
\[
(d,0)(0,0)^L(d,0)
\]
is not admissible: the first anchor forces the intervening hidden state to be
$0$, while the second requires it to be $d$.  Every subword of length at
most $N+1$ meets at most one anchor and is admissible, using the constant
$0$ or constant $d$ hidden path as appropriate.  Thus no finite forbidden
list defines the image.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact finite-block onset, Fischer cover, and Markov order]
\label{thm:quadratic-exact-local-order}
Let $m\ge m_*(\beta)$ and define
\[
\delta(\beta,m)=\min\{n\ge1:\Phi_{\beta,m,n}\text{ is injective}\}.
\]
Then
\[
\delta(\beta,m)=m.
\]
The natural overlap graph with vertex set
$\mathcal A_\beta^{m-1}$ and edge labels $\Fold_{\beta,m}$ is the right
Fischer cover of $Y_{\beta,m}$ and has exactly
$(\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1)^{m-1}$ vertices.  In the output alphabet fixed in
Definition~\ref{def:quadratic-parry-fold}, the image is an $m$-step SFT but
not an $(m-1)$-step SFT.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The upper bound $\delta(\beta,m)\le m$ is
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold}.  For $m\ge3$ the reverse
inequality has a uniform certificate.  In the negative chamber, place the
difference vector $(b,a,-1)$ in raw positions $m-2,m-1,m$ and zeros
elsewhere.  In the positive chamber place
$(b,b-a,1-a,1)$ in positions $m-3,\ldots,m$.  Each vector is the difference
of two digit blocks.  The recurrence shows that all $m-1$ consecutive output
ranks agree modulo $Q_m$, while the raw blocks differ.  For an invertible
aperture $m=2$, the two pairs $(0,0)$ and $(\kappa,d)$ have the same single
output, so again $\delta\ge m$.

The overlap graph is essential and irreducible because its underlying graph
is the full de Bruijn graph.  It is right-resolving: two edges with the same
initial vertex and different appended digits have rank difference
$hQ_{m-1}$ with $1\le|h|\le d$.  We verify that this difference cannot wrap
around the modulus.  In the negative-conjugate chamber,
\[
Q_m=aQ_{m-1}+bQ_{m-2}>aQ_{m-1}=dQ_{m-1}.
\]
In the positive-conjugate chamber $d=a-1$.  For $m=2$,
\[
Q_2=a^2-b>(a-1)a=dQ_1
\]
because $b\le a-2$.  For $m\ge3$, the strict ratio bound
\eqref{eq:ratio-minus} gives
\[
\frac{Q_m}{Q_{m-1}}>a-\frac{b}{a-1}>a-1=d.
\]
Thus $0<|h|Q_{m-1}<Q_m$ in either chamber, proving that the edge labels are
distinct modulo $Q_m$.  It is
left-resolving because two edges with the same terminal vertex and different
initial digits have nonzero rank difference of modulus at most $d<Q_m$.
By $\delta=m$, every output word of length $m$ labels a unique path and is
intrinsically synchronizing.  Distinct vertices have distinct follower
languages: a common right-infinite label would be decoded by
Theorem~\ref{thm:quadratic-optimal-causal-inverse} when $m\ge3$, or by
\eqref{eq:m2-central-decoder}--\eqref{eq:m2-right-decoder} when $m=2$, and
would force the two raw vertices to coincide.  The Fischer-cover criterion
now proves the cover assertion and its state count.

The gluing proof in Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold} defines
$Y_{\beta,m}$ by forbidden output words of length at most $m+1$, so it is an
$m$-step SFT.  The difference certificates above give a length-$(m-1)$
output word which labels two paths ending at distinct Fischer states; for
$m=2$ the same role is played by the common label $(0,0)$.  Write the two
terminal states as $u\ne v$.  Follower-separatedness supplies, after
interchanging $u$ and $v$ if necessary, a successor word
$z\in\mathcal F^+(u)\setminus\mathcal F^+(v)$.  Choose a unique-path
intrinsically synchronizing word ending at the initial state of the path
whose common label terminates at $v$; such a word was constructed in the
Fischer-cover argument above.  Appending the common label to that prefix has
a unique continuation path by right-resolvingness, and that path ends at
$v$.  It therefore cannot be spliced to $z$, although the common label can
be followed by $z$ along the path ending at $u$.  This gives admissible left
and right extensions whose concatenation is not admissible, so the common
word is not intrinsically synchronizing.  Every word of length $r$ in an
$r$-step SFT is intrinsically synchronizing.  Hence $Y_{\beta,m}$ is not an
$(m-1)$-step SFT.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Worked cases in both chambers}

The following computations use the low-to-high convention $(u,v)$ and show
the Parry boundary, the legal rank interval, the cyclic reduction, and the
threshold classification in four genuinely nonmetallic cases.

\begin{example}[Negative conjugate, extremal]
Let $\beta$ be the positive root of $x^2-2x-2$.  Here
$(a,b,d)=(2,2,2)$,
\[
d_\beta^*(1)=(21)^\infty,\qquad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(1,3,8),
\qquad \kappa=b=2=d.
\]
At length two, legality is $v=2\Rightarrow u<2$.  Thus the legal pairs are
\[
(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(0,1),(1,1),(2,1),(0,2),(1,2),
\]
and their ranks $u+3v$ are exactly $0,\ldots,7$.  The raw pair $(2,2)$ has
rank $8$, so cyclic reduction modulo $Q_2=8$ gives
$\Fold_{\beta,2}(2,2)=(0,0)$.  Consequently the constant raw points
$0^{\mathbb Z}$ and $2^{\mathbb Z}$ collide at aperture two.  Theorem
\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold} gives $m_*(\beta)=3$, as predicted by
the negative extremal condition $a=b$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Negative conjugate, nonextremal]
Let $\beta$ be the positive root of $x^2-3x-2$.  Then
$(a,b,d)=(3,2,3)$,
\[
d_\beta^*(1)=(31)^\infty,\qquad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(1,4,14),
\qquad \kappa=b=2<d.
\]
The legal pairs obey $v=3\Rightarrow u<2$; explicitly,
\[
X_2^{(\beta)}=\{0,1,2,3\}\times\{0,1,2\}
\ \cup\ \{(0,3),(1,3)\},
\]
and their ranks $u+4v$ fill $0,\ldots,13$.  The only wrapped pairs are
\[
\Fold_{\beta,2}(2,3)=(0,0),\qquad
\Fold_{\beta,2}(3,3)=(1,0).
\]
For the raw triple $(3,3,0)$ the two outputs are
$y_0=(1,0)$ and $y_1=(3,0)$.  Formula
\eqref{eq:m2-central-decoder} reads $p_1=3\in\{d-\kappa,d\}=\{1,3\}$ and
recovers $a_1=3$; then \eqref{eq:m2-left-decoder} gives
$a_0=1+2=3$, and \eqref{eq:m2-right-decoder} gives $a_2=0$ because
$p_1=a_1$.  Hence the boundary triple is recovered from two outputs and
$m_*(\beta)=2$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Positive conjugate, extremal]
Let $\beta$ be the positive root of $x^2-3x+1$.  Here
$(a,b,d,c_0)=(3,1,2,1)$,
\[
d_\beta^*(1)=21^\infty,\qquad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(1,3,8),
\qquad \kappa=a-b=2=d.
\]
The boundary condition at length two is $v=2\Rightarrow u\le1$.  Hence the
legal pairs are
\[
(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(0,1),(1,1),(2,1),(0,2),(1,2),
\]
with ranks $0,\ldots,7$, while $(2,2)$ has rank $8$ and is recoded to
$(0,0)$.  The constant raw points $0^{\mathbb Z}$ and
$2^{\mathbb Z}$ therefore collide at aperture two.  This is the positive
norm-one extremal family $b=1$, and $m_*(\beta)=3$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Positive conjugate, nonextremal]
Let $\beta$ be the positive root of $x^2-4x+2$.  Then
$(a,b,d,c_0)=(4,2,3,1)$,
\[
d_\beta^*(1)=31^\infty,\qquad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(1,4,14),
\qquad \kappa=a-b=2<d.
\]
The length-two boundary again gives $v=3\Rightarrow u\le1$, so the legal
ranks on
\[
X_2^{(\beta)}=\{0,1,2,3\}\times\{0,1,2\}
\ \cup\ \{(0,3),(1,3)\}
\]
are $0,\ldots,13$, and the wrapped pairs are
$(2,3)\mapsto(0,0)$ and $(3,3)\mapsto(1,0)$.  For the raw triple $(3,3,0)$,
the output pair $((1,0),(3,0))$ is decoded exactly as in the preceding
nonextremal example: $a_1=3$, $a_0=1+\kappa=3$, and $a_2=0$.  Thus the
positive-chamber nonextremal case has $m_*(\beta)=2$.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[What is and is not claimed]
\label{rem:quadratic-open-interface}
The theorem concerns the cyclic language-rank recoding of
Definition~\ref{def:quadratic-parry-fold}.  Published finite-transducer
normalization results for Pisot bases
\cite{Frougny1992,FrougnySteiner2008,BertheFrougnyRigoSakarovitch2019}
establish recognizability for numerical representations on other redundant
digit sets and boundary conventions, but they do not identify those
normalizations with this cyclic rank map.
No threshold claim is made for signed digits, non-greedy expansions,
non-cyclic truncation, degree greater than two, or general Pisot substitution
codings.  These choices are genuine residual interfaces rather than
consequences of Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold}.
\end{remark}

\section{The metallic specialization}
\label{sec:metallic-cover}

Fix $A\ge1$ and let $\beta_A$ be the positive root of $x^2-Ax-1$.  Define
\[
Q_0^{(A)}=1,\qquad Q_1^{(A)}=A+1,
\qquad Q_{j+2}^{(A)}=AQ_{j+1}^{(A)}+Q_j^{(A)}.
\]
On $\mathcal A_A=\{0,\ldots,A\}$, the legal words are
\[
X_m^{(A)}=\{x\in\mathcal A_A^m:
x_k=A\Rightarrow x_{k-1}=0\text{ for }2\le k\le m\},
\]
with colexicographic rank
\[
\Rank_{A,m}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^m x_kQ_{k-1}^{(A)}.
\]
These formulas are the negative-chamber specialization $(a,b)=(A,1)$ of
Definition~\ref{def:quadratic-parry-fold} and
\eqref{eq:qminus}.  They also have the boundary-modified constant-type
interpretation
\[
Q_j^{(A)}=q_j+q_{j-1},
\]
where $q_{j+1}=Aq_j+q_{j-1}$ are the convergent denominators for
$[0;A,A,\ldots]$.  The weights are not the standard Ostrowski weights
$q_j$, and the lowest digit $A$ remains allowed; the model uses the
constant-type local constraint followed by cyclic rank reduction
\cite{HieronymiTerry2018}.

For $A=1$, $Q_j^{(1)}=F_{j+2}$, the legal language is the Fibonacci language,
and the recoding is exactly the map of Sections~\ref{sec:stabilization}--
\ref{sec:stab:branch-and-conjugacy}.  Thus the negative-chamber case $b=1$
in the dual parameterization is already represented by this construction,
while the full quadratic theorem supplies its threshold classification.

\begin{corollary}[Metallic thresholds as a quadratic specialization]
\label{cor:metallic-specialization}
For the preceding rank data, excluding the trivial aperture $m=1$,
\[
\{m\ge2:\Phi_{A,m}\text{ is a topological conjugacy onto }Y_{A,m}\}
=
\begin{cases}
\{3,4,5,\ldots\},&A=1,\\
\{2,3,4,\ldots\},&A\ge2.
\end{cases}
\]
For every aperture in this set and every $n\ge m$, the finite-block map is a
bijection onto its image and
\[
|\mathcal L_n(Y_{A,m})|=(A+1)^{n+m-1}.
\]
Its memory-zero inverse has anticipation at most $m-1$.  The natural overlap
graph is the right Fischer cover in the fixed stabilized alphabet, finite
block injectivity begins exactly at length $m$, and the image is exactly an
$m$-step SFT.  Hence the golden mean is the unique metallic parameter whose
nontrivial threshold is three.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The polynomial $x^2-Ax-1$ is precisely the negative quadratic chamber with
$(a,b)=(A,1)$.  The threshold formula is therefore the specialization of
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-quadratic-pisot-threshold}: it is exceptional exactly
when $A=1$.  The exact finite-block onset, inverse, Fischer-cover, and Markov
order statements follow from
Theorem~\ref{thm:quadratic-exact-local-order}.  The language count is the
cardinality of the full raw block alphabet once the finite-block map is
injective.  In the golden case these identifications agree with
Lemma~\ref{lem:m3-decoder}, Theorem~\ref{thm:block-invertibility}, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:m2-branch-locus}; no separate metallic decoder or
Fischer-cover proof is required.
\end{proof}

Thus two-window rigidity, family block-bijection, and the threshold formula
are all consequences of one quadratic classification.
Likewise, the general Fischer-cover conclusion subsumes the
Fibonacci-specialized cover criterion.  This subsection records the useful
constant-type formulas without duplicating those proofs.

 349: \begin{lemma}[Quadratic bounded sliding congruences]
 350: \label{lem:quadratic-sliding-congruences}
 351: Take either parameter chamber in

 354: $e_0,\ldots,e_{2m-2}\in[-d,d]\cap\mathbb Z$ satisfy

 357: \qquad(0\le t<m),\label{eq:sliding-kernel}

 360: \end{lemma}

 363: Write $s=1$ in the negative chamber and $s=-1$ in the positive chamber, so
 364: $Q_{j+2}=aQ_{j+1}+sbQ_j$, and put

 366: $(d,\delta)=(a-1,0)$ for $s=-1$.  Subtracting $a$ times the congruence at
 367: $t+1$ and $sb$ times that at $t+2$ from the congruence at $t$ cancels every
 368: interior coefficient and gives
 369: \begin{equation}
 370: e_t+\delta e_{t+1}-sbQ_{m-1}e_{t+m+1}\equiv0\pmod{Q_m}.
 371: \label{eq:quadratic-elimination}
 372: \end{equation}

 390: \]

 392: digits vanish.  Back substitution in the preceding congruences then gives

   6: \begin{lemma}[Nearest-multiple separation]
   7: \label{lem:nearest-multiple-separation}
   8: Let $Q_0,Q_1,\ldots$ satisfy either \eqref{eq:qminus} or \eqref{eq:qplus},
   9: write $s=1$ or $s=-1$ accordingly, and put

  13: Then, for $r\ge4$ and $1\le |e|\le d$,
  14: \begin{equation}
  15: \operatorname{dist}(beQ_{r-1},Q_r\mathbb Z)\ge Q_{r-2}.
  16: \label{eq:quadratic-separation}
  17: \end{equation}
  18: \end{lemma}
  19: 
  20: \begin{proof}
  21: Distance is unchanged by replacing $e$ with $-e$, so assume $1\le e\le d$.
  22: Set
  23: \[
  24: R_r:=\frac{Q_{r-1}}{Q_{r-2}}.
  25: \]

  27: ranges imply, by induction,
  28: \begin{align}
  29: a+\frac{b}{a+1}&\le R_r<a+\frac ba &&(s=1,\ r\ge3),
  30: \label{eq:ratio-plus}\\
  31: a-\frac{b}{a-1}&<R_r\le a-\frac ba &&(s=-1,\ r\ge3).
  32: \label{eq:ratio-minus}
  33: \end{align}
  34: For completeness, in the positive-recurrence case the map
  35: $x\mapsto a+b/x$ reverses order, sends
  36: $[a+b/(a+1),a+b/a)$ into itself, and $R_3=a+b/(a+1)$.
  37: In the negative-recurrence case $x\mapsto a-b/x$ preserves order, the interval
  38: in \eqref{eq:ratio-minus} lies in $(a-1,a)$, and $R_3=a-b/a$.
  39: These observations prove the two inductions, including the stated strict
  40: endpoints.
  41:

  48: U_-&:=a-\frac{b}{a-b/a}.
  49: \end{align*}
  50: Thus
  51: \begin{equation}
  52: L_+\le R_r\le U_+\quad(s=1,r\ge4),

  55: \label{eq:sharpened-ratio-bounds}
  56: \end{equation}
  57: The first assertion follows because the order-reversing map interchanges the
  58: endpoints $R_4=U_+$ and $R_5=L_+$ and maps $[L_+,U_+]$ into itself.  The
  59: second follows because $R_3=a-b/a$, $R_4=U_-$, and the increasing map sends
  60: $(L_-,U_-]$ into itself.
